Śrī, Śiva, the Guru, and the Lord Śiva are the refuge of all;
Śiva is the Self, [the source] of all... || 1-1 ||
The creation of the universe is manifold; the activity of Śiva is manifold.
The majesty of Śiva is manifold;
I shall now declare that which is the immediate means for both heaven and liberation.
[On the summit of Mount Meru... 1–4.
Sanatkumāra asked about the duties of Śiva in their proper sequence.
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
The Śivadharma, which is the supreme among all dharmas and whose essence is Śiva,
was formerly proclaimed by Śiva to Pārvatī and to Ṣaṇmukha.
This [is for] the hosts of the chief gods, and especially for us,
and for all living beings submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
This glorious boat of the Śivadharmottara has been proclaimed for the sake of crossing over by those peaceful-minded devotees of Śiva who seek the goal of Śiva. (1.9)
O Rudras, that supreme dharma is practiced by him; there is no doubt about this, whether in a village or in a forest, in water or even on dry land.
Wherever a *liṅga* is found, there indeed are all sacred fords (*tīrthas*);
[one should worship] once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or even constantly.
Those who remember Virūpākṣa should be known as lords of the Gaṇas;
those men who shall glorify Rudra even once will quickly [attain their goal].
They are liberated from all sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes— by that self-betrayer who, once born, has not worshipped the Blessed Lord Śiva.
For a very long time he wanders in this saṃsāra, an ocean of suffering; [this] is the state of equanimity and silence. 1-14.
Whether for a single moment or a muhūrta, one should contemplate Śiva alone;
for having attained this human birth, which is so difficult to obtain... [1.15]
For their birth is indeed fruitful; those best of men have achieved their life's purpose who are devoted to Bhava and whose minds are bowed in salutation to Bhava.
Meditative cultivation... || 1-17 ||
They constantly praise the lotus-feet of Hara;
[they possess] good fortune, radiance, and... || 1-19 ||
For one who worships Śiva, there shall be valor and renown throughout the world;
no one who is not Rudra would remember Rudra, nor would anyone who is not Rudra worship Rudra.
One should not [fail to] attain it;
whether through association, curiosity, greed, or even fear, one should indeed keep it in mind. || 1-21 ||
Whether one recites it or even worships it, he too shall [attain] that [liberation];
this is the essence of the Śiva-dharma: unwavering devotion to Śiva. (1.22)
And that eightfold path has been taught by Śiva; it should be practiced constantly and with effort:
affection for my devotees, worship [of me], and rejoicing in [the worship] of others.
Worshiping me personally with devotion, performing physical gestures for my sake,
devotion while listening to my stories, and the transformation of one's voice, eyes, and limbs [through emotion].
He who constantly remembers me and lives depending upon me—even if he be a barbarian—in whom this eightfold devotion resides. (1.25)

That lord of brahmins, Jvala, though glorious, self-controlled, and learned, is not dear to me even if he knows the four Vedas; whereas one who is my devotee, even if he is an outcaste, is dear to me.
Therefore, one should give to him and receive from him, and he is to be honored just as I am;
for whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— (1.27)
I am never lost to him, nor is he ever lost to me—he who perceives Me as the all-pervading, existing within everything as the soul of all. 1.28
p.
4) Even while searching level ground among mountain fastnesses, one does not see Me;
he who would see Me as all-pervading and everything as established in Me—[he sees]. (1.29)
"He always abides within her, and she always abides within me.
Thus [it is said].
Devotion to Śiva is difficult to attain, and the worship of Śiva is likewise difficult to attain.
O Śivā, the giving of gifts to Śiva is very difficult to obtain; the fire-oblation to Śiva is also difficult to obtain.
The knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to obtain, and its practice is likewise difficult to obtain. (1.31)
One should know that recitation and meditation whose essence is Śiva are extremely difficult to attain; having realized this extreme difficulty, one should take refuge in devotion to Śiva. (1.32)
Blessed are those humans whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward Śiva, both by day and by night. (1.33)
Accompanied by the salutation and other elements, the three syllables "śi-vā-ya" [should be placed] upon the tip of the tongue... [and so forth].
That which was proclaimed in the first chapter of the Śivadharmottara has been thus described. || 1-35 ||
Whoever recites this [attains] wealth,
longevity, fame, knowledge, and incomparable power;
[he dwells] in the presence of Śiva on Kailāsa.
"O best of the sons of the Lotus-born One, you are exceedingly devoted to Śiva. (1.38)
Therefore, I shall tell you everything; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Formerly, when the terrible single ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished—
A very great dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding one another:
"I am the creator," and "I am the creator; there is no other Lord of the universe greater than me."
Thus Brahmā spoke to Hari, and likewise Hari to Brahmā,
for the purpose of removing the pride of those two gods and for their spiritual awakening.
In the center, the supreme linga of the Lord’s splendor has arisen—divine, consisting of garlands of flames, immeasurable, and peerless. (1.42)
It stands in pure water, extending for ten thousand yojanas;
it is free from decay and growth, and devoid of beginning, middle, or end. (1.43)
Deluded by the flames of that *liṅga*, those two best of gods, the lords of the immortals,
were then struck with wonder as they gazed upon it.
Having deliberated with one another regarding his upward and downward movements,
Viṣṇu went to look below and the Grandfather (Brahmā) went upwards.
Not seeing either the lower or the upper limit, the two met with one another,
joined their palms in reverence, and then praised the Liṅga.
Salutations to you, whose mark is knowledge, the Śiva-liṅga, the possessor of the liṅga;
salutations to you, whose liṅga is hidden, the supreme liṅga, the radiant one.
Salutations to you, the light-form, the Veda-form, the Creator;
salutations to you, the subtle form, the intellect-form, and the Intellect itself. (1.48)
Salutations to you who are the Linga of the mountain, salutations to you who are the Linga of existence;
salutations to the Linga that is the cause of the universe, salutations to the Lord of the worlds.
"Salutations to the Lord of us two, and salutations to the Lord of lords.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, the two of them bowed their heads to him.
Endowed with supreme devotion, Brahmā and Viṣṇu beheld the Supreme,
situated within the center of the Liṅga, measuring a span.
Endowed with the perfection of meditative concentration, they beheld that which is of the nature of Śiva;
yet this was neither gold, nor silver, nor copper, nor crystal, nor pearl.
Abiding solely within the object of perception, peaceful and absolute, that [state] is of the nature of Śiva.
Mahādeva, pleased with those two, granted them an excellent boon.
Having acknowledged his status as the cause,
the sages then praised that very place; they extolled the Linga as an imitation of his own characteristics,
and [praised] the supreme, hidden body and the Linga-kṣetra.
At the end of the kalpa, all the deities dissolve into that linga.
Brahmā dissolves into the right, and [Viṣṇu] into the left;
the Vedas, together with their phonemes, accents, words, and krama-readings, dissolve indeed into the head.
The entire world dissolves within his belly... || 1.58 ||
Everything established by him would be worshipped; of this there is no doubt. || 1-59 ||
Formerly, [the gods] fashioned the Liṅga and the Cakra with equal [care].
Brahmā always worships the Liṅga with divine, sacred syllables (brahmākṣara).

By constantly worshipping Viṣṇu with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he attained the supreme state of Brahman through that complete adoration. Śakra also, the lord of the gods and kings... [62]
The giver of wealth always worships a beautiful linga made of gold.
By that [act], he obtained wealth...
the high-souled Viśvedevas [bestowed] a beautiful silver linga.
By worshipping with devotion according to the prescribed rites,
Viṣṇu attained through Vāyu the state of being the universe, which brings incomparable qualities;
he always worships that Liṅga made of sapphire.
By that means, he attained the singular, eternal state of Viṣṇu. (p.
8) The Vasus worship the bell-metal Liṅga according to the prescribed rites. (1.67)
By that means, those great-souled ones attained the status of Vasus and great prosperity,
while worshipping the earthly linga of the Aśvins according to the prescribed rites.
By that [merit], both the Aśvin gods attained divine bodies;
Varuṇa always worships a pure crystal liṅga.
By him, that state of Varuṇa was indeed attained, endowed with prosperity;
having worshipped the auspicious *liṅga* composed of food (*annamaya*), Agni was purified by his devotion.
Soma always worships a linga made of pearls;
by that, Soma attained his ever-shining state as the Moon (Somatva).
The best of the serpents worship a linga made of coral;
by that means, they have attained the supreme state, becoming rich in enjoyments among the Nāgas.
The best of the asuras and the high-souled rākṣasas, whose prowess was sharpened by him, worshipped the emblem (liṅga) of Kṛṣṇa according to the established rule.
The Piśācas worship a liṅga made of cucumber;
possessing great power and majesty, they attain the supreme state. || 1.74 ||
The best among householders worship a linga made of black iron or a linga composed of three metals;
endowed with the power of yoga through that, they go to the abode of the Lord. (1.75)
Having moved from one spot to another, with hands free from movement,
accompanied by verbal praise and mental meditation— this is the four-limbed circumambulation.
With the chest, the head, devotion, the mind, the intellect,
the eyes, the feet, the two arms, and speech— this is called the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*).
The Mothers always worship a linga made largely of iron;
having attained motherhood, they all proceed to the supreme state. (1.76)
Thus the gods, together with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
always worship Īśāna, the leader of the deities.
The entire world consists of the *liṅga*; everything is established in the *liṅga*.
Therefore, one should worship the *liṅga* if one desires one's own spiritual perfection (*siddhi*). (1.78)
Thus ends the second chapter of the Śivadharmottara.
p. 10) Śrī. Now begins the third chapter.
Within the *liṅga*, the Great God Mahādeva is himself directly present for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*. (2-1)
He who, out of delusion, does not worship the Linga, the Lord of the three worlds, is not a recipient of heaven, nor of liberation, nor of sovereignty. (2-2)
But he who constantly worships the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds, quickly becomes a recipient of heaven, liberation, and sovereignty. (2-3)
Therefore, having become single-minded, the wise man, even when fallen into distress, should always worship Mahādeva for as long as he lives, according to his vow. (2.4)
Better is the abandonment of life, or even the cutting off of one's head,
than that one should eat without having first worshipped the Blessed Three-eyed One.
He who carries this out for as long as he lives according to his vow, though bound by human skin, is indeed Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. (2-6)
"There is no merit anywhere else that is greater than the worship of the Liṅga;
having realized this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort. (2.7)
If a man, out of hatred or delusion, reviles the Liṅga worshipped by all the gods, he shall go to hell—even by merely conversing with him. (2.8)
The entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, consists of Maheśvara.
Those who have become devotees of Maheśvara are, in this world, [truly] ungrateful [for their own attainment]. (2.9)
The oceans may come to an end, and even the Himalayas may waste away;
yet there is no exhaustion in the world of Rudra for one who has gone for refuge to Śaṅkara.
One should desire many sons who follow the Śiva-tantras;
they rescue their lineage just as a rope [rescues] a jar from a well. (2-11)
Two types of linga have been fully described: the moving and the non-moving.
The moving is renowned as the "pratīti" (the conceptual), while the non-moving is of the nature of earth.
In the moving [body], Maheśvara always dwells indeed, ever-yoked;
in the non-moving, Sadāśiva always dwells through the consecration of mantra. || 2-13 ||
The *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: the stationary (*sthāvara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*). Through the neglect of the moving one, the stationary becomes fruitless. (2.14)
Having thus established the *liṅga*, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva within it;
this is his meditation: his divine form is adorned with a crescent moon. (2.15)
His throat was dark as the tamāla tree, his brow and eyes were quivering,
his left side shone with a woman, and he wore the auspicious armlet of the serpent Śeṣa.
He whose matted locks are perpetually washed by contact with the waves of the Gaṅgā,
and whose radiant limbs are honored by the mass of pollen from the bodies of the gods.
His limbs were adorned with various ornaments, and he was decorated with great serpents;
mounted upon a magnificent bull as his vehicle, he held the Ājagava bow as his weapon. (2.18)
[He] who has an elephant hide as his upper garment, who has five faces, [and is] Guha;
who provides protection for those seeking refuge, who is the cause of liberation for those who bow [before him],
who transcends the path of the mind's desires, and who is devoted to the granting of boons.
Having thus meditated upon Mahādeva, one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga);
therein, having mentally fashioned the ritual substances and purified them.
Having meditated upon the god Vināyaka and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
one should likewise worship Nandīśa in the south and Suyaśas in the north.
Having properly propitiated him with the mind, one should then prepare a seat;
upon that, one should meditate on Śiva, accompanied by Ambā and enchanting to all.
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautiful in every limb,
possessed of every excellence, and adorned with all ornaments.
With red face, hands, and feet, his countenance bears a gentle smile like a kunda flower;
he resembles pure crystal and has three eyes like blooming lotuses.
Hara has four arms and noble limbs, bears the beautiful crescent moon, holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands, and carries a deer and an axe.
The abode of all that is auspicious, with its beautiful blue throat, beyond all comparison, accompanied by his followers and his retinue. (2.27)
Then, one should meditate upon Maheśvarī on his left side,
with wide and long eyes resembling the petals of a full-blown lotus. (2-28)
Her face has the luster of the full moon, her hair on the head is dark blue,
she resembles the petals of a blue lotus, and she has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She possessed breasts that were exceedingly round, firm, high, smooth, and full;
she had a slender waist and broad hips, and was dressed in very fine yellow garments.
She was endowed with all ornaments, radiant with a tilaka mark upon her forehead, and graced by a mass of hair strewn with various flowers. || 2-31 ||
Her form was entirely graceful, her face slightly downcast with modesty, and she held a blooming golden lotus in her right hand.
And likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord and the Goddess seated together on a splendid, excellent throne, with the other [the Goddess] placing her hand like a staff [upon his knee]. (2.33)

One should worship with devotion using all ritual offerings and flowers of inner sentiment; having meditated according to the external sequence, one should indeed perform the worship through the intellect.
Thereafter, one should visualize the oblation in the navel with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and other offerings;
and one should meditate on Śiva between the eyebrows, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp. (2–35)
Then, having completed the entire sequence of propitiation consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*),
one should worship the God, the crest-jewel of all deities, within the *liṅga*.
Some [worship] the god Viśveśvara, some that which is known as Hālāsya,
some the one called Śrīsomanātha, and some the wonderful Kedāra.
Some consider Śrīparvata to be the foremost, some men [consider] Goparvata;
some [consider] Dakṣiṇakailāsa, and others the one named Vṛddhācala.
Some, having reached the meritorious and wonderful Rāmeśvara in the forest of the Vedas by the previously mentioned path,
and having worshipped it by the previously mentioned path...
O best of the twice-born! (2-39)
They shall be liberated from saṃsāra and the bonds of existence without effort;
what is the use of much speaking here? Listen, O bulls among sages! (2.40)
Worship Mahādeva, the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for when the ancient Lord of the gods of gods is worshipped, he is the benefactor of all.
"And all the gods are worshipped"—such is the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta. (2.40)
His eastern face is gentle, with a luster like that of the rising sun;
it is enriched by three lotus-like eyes and adorned with the young moon as its crest-ornament.
With a radiant luster like that of a southern dark-blue cloud,
his face was terrible with a frowning brow and possessed three red, circular eyes.
His fangs were formidable and terrifying, his sprout-like lower lip quivered,
he wore a crescent moon as a crest-ornament, and his hair blazed upward.
The northern face was renowned for its prowess, adorned with dark locks of hair,
playful, three-eyed, and radiant with its moon-ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon, radiant with three eyes;
it bears the crescent moon, is gentle, and is enchanting with a subtle smile. (2.45)
The western face resembles crystal, radiant as the crescent of the moon;
it is exceedingly gentle and brilliant with three wide-open eyes.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Śivadharmottara.
p. 15) Śrī! Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Rudrākṣa trees are born from the Sun’s eye;
they have twelve faces and are distinguished by tawny varieties.
Those born from the Moon’s eye are sixteen-faced and white in color.
Kṛṣṇa, desiring to give [them] away, [gave them] those born from Jvalanākṣi. || 3-1 ||
The Brahmin seed is white, endowed with the color of Kapila;
the Kṣatriya is indeed Vaiśya, for it is of a dual nature;
they declare the Śūdra seed to be black.
The origin of the rudrākṣa seed is indeed by birth. || 3-2 ||
The single-faced Rudrākṣa seed is Śaṅkara himself in person; it destroys the sin of killing.
The two-faced seed destroys the sin of slaughtering many cows.
It has the Lord of Gods as its deity and is unattainable for the eyes.
May that [face] which is said to be of Agni, possessing three mouths that instantly destroy the killing of women,
and that four-faced one which is worthy of being praised by the four-faced [Brahmā], [grant us success].
It destroys the sin of killing a human being in an instant. || 3-4 ||
But the five-faced Kālāgni destroys the sins arising from the consumption of forbidden food and the company of the wicked.
For that Skanda who has six faces was indeed held in his hand by Nara in the midst of those who slay the twice-born.
The seven-faced image of Ananta, the lord of serpents, immediately effects purification from theft;
likewise, a golden eight-faced image of Vaināyaka.
The *kūṭa* [mantra] destroys sins such as approaching the wife of one's guru. 3-6.
The god Bhairava himself,
holding your face with his left hand, bestows enjoyment, liberation, and fame equal to that of Śiva.
He destroys ten million times ten thousand murders. || 3-7 ||
Take up for yourself that seed-syllable of the Ten-faced One (Daśavaktra),
by which Piśācas, Bhūtas, Grahas, Rākṣasas, Vetālas, serpents, adversaries, and lions [are overcome].
And it swiftly destroys those [obstacles] beginning with Vyādhi.
One should, according to the faultless rite, wear upon the crest the eleven-faced [form] and the single Raudra [face],
which is equal to ten thousand human and horse sacrifices and Vājapeyas.
It is equal to a thousand gifts of a thousand cows. || 3-9 ||
That which was spoken by the twenty mouths is known as the Bhāskarīya; it resides in the throat and brings satisfaction to the Sun,
equal to the merit of sacrifices performed with horses, elephants, and dogs.
It removes the defects caused by jackals, mice, birds, eunuchs, barren women, deer, serpents, parrots, frogs, snakes, buffaloes, hunters, and those afflicted by poison. (3-10)
If one does not obtain the twenty faces, that is remembered as Kārttikeya;

everything is accomplished, and all objects of enjoyment shall be attained through that *pādukā*. This is the practice for attaining desired goals, the essence of the nectar, and the mother of the noble embryo.
One who lives with his father, brother, or wife becomes purified; there is nothing higher than this.
Even a single rudrākṣa may be worn on the crest-lock,
while a garland of thirty-six should be placed upon the head; and with thirty-two beads, the goal is to be accomplished on the pair of ears.
A rosary for the heart consists of fifty beads. || 3-12 ||
He who always wears an akṣamālā around his neck and recites [mantras] shall obtain the merit of a thousand sacrifices;
it is prescribed as white, red, yellow, or black for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
Just as one might not obtain a rudrākṣa, so too this [mantra] should be worn upon the crest-lock or on the hand.

Who indeed would not be irreproachable when, during bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, the performance of vows, worship of the deity, or giving of gifts, they bind [the sacred thread] around the neck, the pair of ears, and the heart with silver and other materials, using the mantras consisting of the five-syllable Praṇava?
Having performed the initiation and the ancestral rites (śrāddha), he [should be] smeared with ashes and wear a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
One should perform whatever action there may be so that its fruit becomes entirely inexhaustible;
otherwise, this [action] becomes useless, and alas, this faultless [act] would surely become a sin.

Some do not wear their rosaries or food during childbirth, the death of a child, or the evacuation of excrement, nor when in contact with women, for fear that it might cause the loss of longevity. (3-15)
Others say that one should always wear on the arm or on the ears a sin-destroying rosary while reciting the mantra; however, a very large garland should not be worn during purification.
Even a most sinful man becomes pure if he wears even a single bead.
Even while acting, he is not tainted by those improper things censured from various quarters. || 3-16 ||

By joining tail to tail and mouth to mouth with their counterparts, and wearing golden beads interspersed with pearls and corals, a mortal who partakes of the fruit of sacrifice becomes irreproachable.
If one wears a rudrākṣa upon the body, even a dead dog would be liberated.
Eating during the final muhūrta, he shall go to the city of Śiva; he is not born again.

O Sage, what is the use of many spoken words? I shall tell you this faultless truth for you: a person who always wears this mantra-empowered rudrākṣa upon his own body does not return again to saṃsāra. O Lord, having bound the rudrākṣa with gold or silver, O Sage...
One should always wear it on the tuft of hair or on the ears, being composed in mind.
A man, with the sacred thread held in his hand or around his neck, should [wear it] either with the glorious five-syllabled mantra or with the *praṇava* alone. (3-19)
The wise man should joyfully wear Rudrākṣa beads with his own mantra;
the wearing of Rudrākṣa is the direct means for attaining the knowledge of Śiva. (3-20)
The wearing of Rudrākṣas by those in all stages of life (āśramas) and all castes (varṇas) is prescribed;
however, it must be performed with the recitation of mantras for the twice-born (dvijas), and not for those of other castes. (3.21)
O great sage, for those who feel shame in wearing rudrākṣa beads, there is no liberation from saṃsāra even after ten million births. (3-22)
It is certain that for one who speaks ill upon seeing a wearer of rudrākṣa beads, there is indeed a mixture of castes (saṃkara) in his own birth. (3-23)
Whether it be without mantra or accompanied by mantra, devoid of [mental] cultivation—
whoever that man may be who would always wear it, free from shame— (3.24)
Freed from all sins, one shall attain perfect knowledge;
oh, the majesty of the rudrākṣa! It is impossible for me to describe it fully.
Therefore, you should wear rudrākṣas with every effort;
for that reason, the wearing of rudrākṣas should always be performed by everyone. (3-26)
This [practice] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and it has always been maintained by me;
there is nothing superior to the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads found here in this world. (3-27)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Śivadharma.
p. 20) Śrī: Now begins the fifth chapter.
O Lord! O Śiva, destroyer of Tripura, primordial God, Śambhu! O three-eyed Śaṅkara, Rudra, wielder of the trident!
Those who utter "Be my refuge" in this world— [may they be protected by you].
Those men do not fall into the ocean of existence. || 4-1 ||
In the Śaiva tradition: "Oṃ, salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha"—this mantra of eight meritorious syllables liberates one even from great sins if recited just once. (4.2)
The chanting of "Mahādeva" is a ladder for ascending to heaven, made firm by the nine oceans as its rungs.
Indeed, the glorification of Mahādeva is the liberation from bonds, the medicine for the blind and the destitute, and the place of refuge for the wretched. (4-4)
O Mahādeva! The creeper of speech, with its four-syllable sprouts, when watered with devotion, bears fruit—indeed, the fruits of the four aims of human life. 4-5.
This sound—"Mahādeva, Mahādeva, Mahādeva!"—is the drumbeat for the wise to take the hand of the bride that is liberation. (4.6)
Tens of millions of sins of killing a Brahmin and tens of millions of sins of incestuous unions undergo immediate dissolution through the cry of "O Mahādeva! 4-7.
For one in whose speech the auspicious name "Śiva" proceeds,
millions of great sins are instantly reduced to ashes. (4.8)
The two syllables "Śi-va" are the provisions for the journey of the life-breath at death, the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, and the pacifier of infinite suffering. (4.9)
The word "Śiva" exists, and speech is under one's control;
nevertheless, that mortals fall into hell is an act of extreme rashness. (4.10)
O Śivā, even if a Caṇḍāla should daily utter the three words with joy,
one should endure him and always dwell together with him.
Whether out of incidental association, curiosity, greed, fear, or even ignorance, a mortal who utters the name "Hara" is liberated from all sins. (4.2)
By uttering once, "Bring! Strike! Seize! with his weapons, one is liberated;
indeed, the constant chanting of the name of the Lord of Umā releases one from innate desire and karma. (4.13)
First, the three syllables "namaḥ śivāya" should be employed;
he upon whose tongue these reside has a life that is truly fruitful. (4.14)
But for him in whose heart this mantra "Namaḥ śivāya" resides, there is no need for many mantras or for weapons of great elaboration. (4.15)
By him everything has been studied and heard, and by him everything has been practiced, he for whom the practice of the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya" has been made firm. (4.16)
He who beholds the Lord of the gods of gods, in the form of the Śiva-liṅga, at dawn, attains the highest state, which is superior to all others.
By beholding Mahādeva at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice; by beholding him in the evening, having attained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is liberated. (4.18)
One should not look upon Hari at dusk, especially on the thirteenth lunar day;
if one should look upon him out of negligence, there will be a loss of [the merit of] twelve years of bull-vows.
Likewise, having seen the Three-eyed Lord with offerings on the night of the thirteenth day,
one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is liberated from all sins.
Whatever merit is obtained by bathing at numerous sacred fords such as Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Kedāra, and Naimiṣa, one obtains that very merit simply by beholding Śiva. (4.21)
Whether impure or pure, even if one has fallen into any state whatsoever, whoever constantly remembers Rudra is undoubtedly purified; of this there is no doubt. (4.22)
Those who desire great enjoyments, sovereignty, or even the abode of the thirty gods,
should always worship with devotion the lotus feet of Hara.
Brahmā’s role as the creator, Viṣṇu’s crushing of the demons, Indra’s sovereignty over heaven, and the fruit of the ritual worship of Śiva—[all these result from this]. (4.24)
Good fortune, a beautiful form, truthfulness, renunciation, eloquence, heroism, and fame throughout the world—these are the fruits of the rite of worshiping Śiva. (4.25)
At whose gate there are rutting elephants and horses with the speed of the wind, and noble ladies with faces like the full moon—[he attains] the fruit of Śiva... 4.26.
Pleasant dwellings, knowledge, wisdom, delight in Śiva, and wealth whose limit is unseen—these are the fruits of Śiva. (4.27)
Longevity, health, sovereignty, virtuous sons, the abundance of happiness, heaven, liberation, and merit— this is the fruit [of Śiva]. (4.28)
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* shall not be stained by the faults arising from great sins (*mahāpātaka*),
just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Even very many sins, though equal in magnitude to Mount Meru or Mandara,
perish upon encountering the Lord as their physician, like malignant diseases.
For the prosperities of the body are indeed fraught with peril; successes are the very seat of misfortunes;
meetings end in departures; everything is fragile by its very nature of arising.
Rebirth, repeated death, and the succession of afflictions follow the logic of a water-mill; this state has never been otherwise. (4.32)
The fruit of performing austerities on Mount Meru, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, at Naimiṣa, and on the Himavat mountains, is obtained through the worship of the Liṅga.
What is the use here of many garlands of books? In brief, it is taught:
people who have abandoned all worldly activities worship the Lord. (4.34)
"What is the use of all the sciences and scriptures, or of gifts, sacrifices, vows, and the like?
Śiva should be worshipped constantly—this is the supreme instruction. (4.35)
This alone is the supreme Dharma, and Sadāśiva is worshipped;
for this indeed is the knowledge of Śiva, and this indeed is the highest state.

Īśvara said: O great sage, know that *bhasma* (ashes) is the Supreme Brahman, truth, non-dual consciousness and bliss; for it is through the application of ashes (*bhatsanāt*) that all sins and bonds are destroyed. (4.37)
It is called *rakṣā* because it protects from fears; likewise, it is *bhasita* because it illuminates;
and it is designated as *kṣāra* because it cauterizes all defects. (4-38)
"O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, know that there are various secondary [fires], O Sage;
just as there is the fire of the Agnihotra and the fire born of living beings, so too is the fire born of the Virajā oblation. (4.39)
For householders, the fire produced from the *aupāsana* rite is prescribed; for students (*brahmacārin*), the fire produced from the *samit* wood is to be maintained. (4.40)
For Śūdras, [the fire] produced from the cooking fire in the house of a learned Brāhmaṇa (śrotriya) should be maintained;
for all others as well, [the fire] produced from a forest conflagration (dāvānala) should be maintained.
O great sage, [one should apply it] with the five-syllable mantra joined with the *praṇava* on the forehead, the heart, and indeed on both arms.
One who is a householder or a forest-dweller should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), O observer of good vows; it is likewise for all others, even without the recitation of a mantra.
"O Sage, the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be performed with devotion.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Śivadharmottara.
